drills.coachNote: White's rook on d1 is aimed straight down the open d-file at your queen on d3, so sitting still wasn't an option. Qxa3 sidesteps the attack but only nets a stray pawn, and after Qxf5, Qxb4, Rc1 and Qf4 your queen gets chased around while White claws pawns back — over two pawns of your lead gone. The sharp answer was Qxd1, eating the attacking rook itself: after Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 you've swapped queens and come out a full rook up for a bishop, strolling toward a won ending with e4 and Nd4. drills.coachNote: White's queen on a5 is ready to crash in with Qxc7, skewering your bishop on b7 and the rook sitting behind it on d8 — that pawn was going to fall regardless. Qb6 just shuffles your queen to guard things passively, and it let White's knight spring to f5 and grab the initiative, swinging the evaluation by almost four pawns against you. Qe3 was the braver answer: you let Qxc7 happen but hit straight back with Qxd3+, forking White's exposed king on b1 with check, and after Ka1 Rd7 Qe5 you're fully active again. drills.coachNote: Black's bishop on g6 is already staring down the long diagonal at your bishop on d3, and your queen on d1 is the only thing defending it. drills.coachNote: Black's bishop on d6 was already attacking your f4 bishop, so you tried to sidestep by dropping it back to h2 — but h2 sits on that exact same diagonal, so Bxh2+ simply followed you there, and after Kxh2 you'd given away a whole bishop for free, cutting your huge +4.6 lead by 3.6 pawns. The retreat never actually escaped the attack. The real answer was to ignore the bishop: Nb5! swings toward a7, and after Bxf4 Nxa7+ you fork Black's king on c8 and grab the a7 pawn with check — even once exf4 recaptures, you're up a pawn with Black's king badly placed. drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6 wants to swing to b8 with check, and your rook on h8 is left undefended if your king and knight get tangled sorting it out. Kd8 walked straight into Rb8+; you had to block with Nc8, then c6 followed and Rh7 picked off your rook on h8 for free, turning a fighting -2.7 into a crushing +5 for White. Kc8 sidesteps the check entirely — your king stays off the back-rank skewer, and even though White still nets the knight after c6 Bc4 dxe7, you hold on with Kc7 and Rb7+ instead of losing material outright. Check for checks before you move your king.

drills.coachNote: White's pawns on d5 and e5 look imposing, but neither is actually defended — the idea is just to keep rolling them while grabbing your c5 pawn with Rxc5 if you give a free tempo. Kd7 did exactly that: it ignored the hanging d5 pawn, so White played Rxc5, met Rc8, then e6+ kicked your king back to d8, handing White connected passers on d5/e6 and swinging the game from equal toward losing. Nxd5 was sitting there instead — your knight on e7 grabs the pawn free, and after Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6 material evens out again. Check for hanging pawns before marching your king forward.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White is hoping you grab material instead of finishing him off — his king on g1 is nearly mated already, boxed in by your rook on f2 and bishop on e5. You played Rxb2, snatching a pawn, and that let White scramble with Nd2, Qc2, and Rh2, turning a forced mate into merely +5 — still winning, but you gave back an entire mate. Qg2# was there instead: your queen slides down the c6-g2 diagonal, shielded by your rook on f2, and the king on g1 has no flight square and no capture available. When your pieces swarm the enemy king like this, scan for mate before grabbing a free pawn.

drills.coachNote: White has no real threats here — his rook on h1 and knight on b1 sit undeveloped, and his only hope is that you hand him time to untangle with Re1 and b3. Your move a6 did just that: it challenged nothing, so White played Re1, traded down with Rde8, and solidified with b3, shrinking your edge from +4.8 to around +3 even though nothing was lost outright. Qf3 kept the pressure on instead — your queen jumps into White's position eyeing the rook on h1 and king on h2, and after Rd1 Rde8 Re1 Bd6 a4 you're still dictating play. When you're completely winning, keep creating problems rather than passing with moves like a6.

Qb3 actually addressed it, covering the key squares so that even after Rxb2 Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 you simplify into a tough-but-survivable endgame instead of a collapse. Your move b6 ignored it completely, so White kept that knight planted, regrouped with Ng3 and later Ng4, and even with nothing lost outright your edge shrank from +1.7 to barely +0.3. Bxf5 deals with it directly — your bishop on e6 trades it off, and after exf5 Qd7 Nh4 Nd4 Be3 you're left with the better minors and no outpost to worry about. drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Your pawn on c6 is one of your biggest trumps here, and Black's whole plan is just to shuffle his king between e7 and f7 hoping you misplace yours while escorting it home. You played Kf4, and though the game continued Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 Kf7 and you still won, that square cost a good chunk of your edge (+19.8 down to roughly +9) since it's less useful than Kf3 for supporting the e3-e4 push and staying close to the queenside pawns. Kf3 keeps your king centralized and flexible, ready to swing either direction. When you're completely winning, every king move should ask which square serves both sides of the board, not just which looks fine.
drills.threat: Black's king can only shuffle between e7 and f7 — every one of his pawns is fixed in place.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: This endgame wins almost by zugzwang alone - Black's king can only shuffle between e7 and f7, waiting for you to misplace a piece. Putting your bishop on b3 instead of a2 gave Black's king an extra tempo in that shuffle (Ke7, Kc4, Kf7...), which is why the evaluation dropped nearly 10 pawns even though you're still winning. Ba2 sits on the same diagonal but doesn't let Black's king harass it, so your own king is free to march forward - Kc4, then Kb5 - and squeeze him back toward d8. In these pure zugzwang endings, it's not which diagonal, it's the exact square that counts.
drills.threat: Black's king just shuffles between e7 and f7; your winning plan hinges on which square the bishop lands on.

drills.coachNote: Black's attack is one move from landing: with the queen on g5 and rook on f2 both covering d2 and your king on e1, he's threatening mate on d2. Rf1 ignores that and only pins the rook - after Rf1, Black just plays Qxd2#, since your king has no square left and nothing can interpose. You were still up material and fine; the fix was Qd7+, a check that buys a free tempo by forcing the king to move, after which O-O-O tucks your king safely on the queenside (Qd7+ Kf6 O-O-O Bh6 Kb1). When your king's stuck in the center, a forcing check to safety beats a quiet developing move every time.

drills.coachNote: White's a6 and b6 pawns are the real danger - they're marching toward promotion while his king just needs to dodge a check or two to escort them home. Rc1 instead gets your rook behind the pawn - Rc1 b7 Re1+ Kd5 Rb1 - blockading it from the rear while your king comes up to help (Rc6 next). Against a passed pawn, get behind it rather than spending moves on checks that don't slow it down.

drills.coachNote: White's actual plan is Qg7# - the queen on h6 and the bishop on e5 both cover that square, and your king on h8 would have nowhere to go. Rh7 does stop that mate, but it strips the defender off your rook on f8, and White simply plays Qxf8+ instead - with your own rook blocking h7, your king has no escape and it's mate. Qh7 solves the same problem more safely: it's defended by your king, so if White takes, Qxh7+ Kxh7 just trades queens and removes the attacker (Bf4 Re8 Rxe8 keeps things even after). When you block a mating threat, check that the piece you're moving wasn't defending something else first.

Kg8 ignored all of that; it didn't touch the hanging bishop and let White's attack roll on, swinging the evaluation nearly 18 pawns from winning to losing.
